- The first experiment resulted in very similar NLL values for most models (ranging from -21.1 to -22.7), indicating that a single condition with moderate catalyst and high substrate is insufficient to separate them. M20 is clearly a poor fit, and M14, M16, M17, M7 are slightly less likely.
- The top models include second-order catalyst mechanisms (M5, M3), catalyst activation (M6, M8), and various deactivation/inhibition routes.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but the models remain highly degenerate under these conditions. We need to probe a different regime to break this degeneracy.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the degeneracy, especially between first-order and second-order catalyst dependencies, I propose an experiment with the maximum allowed catalyst concentration ([cat]0 = 0.20).
1. By increasing [cat]0 by 4x compared to the first run, mechanisms involving catalyst dimerization (M2, M3, M13) or second-order catalytic steps (M5, M18, M19) will exhibit a strongly non-linear rate or deactivation response compared to first-order models (M1, M6, M8, M9).
2. I also propose lowering the substrate concentration to [S]0 = 1.0. This reduces the S:cat ratio from 40:1 to 5:1, shifting the steady-state distribution of the catalyst to include significantly more free 'cat'. This will help distinguish mechanisms where free catalyst deactivates or reacts (M9, M11, M13) from those where the substrate-bound catalyst deactivates (M14, M16, M18).
3. Setting [P]0 = 0.0 removes initial product inhibition/deactivation, providing a clean contrast to the first experiment to isolate the effects of [cat] and [S].
</hypothesis>
